segments.text: International law also regulates economic relations involving trade, investment, state property and cross-border economic activity.
At CSS level, focus on sovereignty over resources, treatment of foreign economic interests, expropriation, investment obligations and institutional regulation rather than technical trade-law detail.

States possess broad authority to regulate economic activity and natural resources within their jurisdiction, but that authority can be limited by treaties, contracts, customary rules and specific commitments to foreign investors or trading partners. International economic law therefore examines the interaction between regulatory sovereignty and cross-border obligations.

A useful distinction is between the state's general power to regulate and a specific undertaking it has accepted. The existence of foreign investment does not freeze domestic law, but particular treaties may require standards such as non-discrimination, fair treatment or compensation for expropriation.

Foreign-investment disputes often ask whether an investment is protected, whether the state measure falls within the treaty, whether treatment was discriminatory or arbitrary, whether an expropriation occurred, and what remedy is available. Direct expropriation involves formal taking; indirect expropriation concerns measures that substantially deprive an investment of value or control under the applicable legal test.

Compensation questions depend on the governing legal instrument. Students should avoid repeating a universal compensation formula without identifying the treaty, contract or customary rule being applied.

Trade and investment regimes are institutionally distinct. WTO law concerns multilateral trade disciplines among members. Investment protection commonly arises through bilateral or multilateral investment treaties and may use investor-state arbitration where consent exists. International financial institutions operate under their own constituent agreements.

items.text: This area connects sovereignty with cross-border economic obligations. States may regulate resources and economic activity, but they may also be bound by treaties, contracts and international standards.
Foreign investment questions often involve admission of investment, treatment after admission, expropriation, compensation, dispute settlement and state regulatory powers.

Expropriation means state taking or serious deprivation of property interests. The legal consequences depend on the governing treaty or rule, public purpose, non-discrimination, due process and compensation requirements where applicable.
Keep general public international law separate from highly technical trade or investment rules unless the question specifically requires those details.

rows: Common confusion to avoid: Do not imply that economic sovereignty cancels every international commitment. Sovereignty is exercised within obligations the state has accepted or that otherwise bind it.

items.text: Link the topic to state sovereignty and responsibility.
Prepare lawful expropriation and compensation at a general level.

segments.text: Economic sovereignty exists within international obligations.
Foreign investment disputes often combine treaty rules, domestic law and arbitration.
